Before starting a patient on biologic DMARDs (e.g., TNF-α inhibitors) for RA, what screening must be performed?
a: Screening for latent tuberculosis (e.g., PPD or IFN-γ release assay) and Hepatitis B and C.

q: What is the classic radiographic finding in Osteoarthritis?
a: Joint space narrowing, subchondral sclerosis, subchondral cysts, and osteophytes.

q: What is the characteristic hand joint involvement in Osteoarthritis?
a: DIP joints (Heberden nodes), PIP joints (Bouchard nodes), and the first carpometacarpal (CMC) joint.

What is the classic triad of Reactive Arthritis?
a: Urethritis, conjunctivitis, and oligoarthritis ("can't see, can't pee, can't climb a tree").

q: What common infections precipitate Reactive Arthritis?
a: Gastrointestinal infections (Salmonella, Shigella, Campylobacter) or genitourinary infections (Chlamydia trachomatis).

What type of crystals are seen in Gout upon synovial fluid analysis?
a: Monosodium urate crystals, which are needle-shaped and strongly negatively birefringent (yellow when parallel to the compensator axis).

q: What is the mechanism of action of allopurinol used in chronic gout management?
a: Xanthine oxidase inhibitor, which decreases uric acid production.

q: In a patient with an acute gout flare who has chronic kidney disease, what is the best treatment option?
a: Intra-articular or systemic glucocorticoids (NSAIDs and colchicine are contraindicated or require caution in severe CKD).

q: What type of crystals are seen in Pseudogout (CPPD) upon synovial fluid analysis?
a: Calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate (Ca<sub>2</sub>P<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub>) crystals, which are rhomboid-shaped and weakly positively birefringent (blue when parallel to the compensator axis).

q: What radiographic finding in the knee is highly suggestive of Pseudogout?
a: Chondrocalcinosis (calcification of the articular cartilage or meniscus).

What is the most serious complication of Giant Cell Arteritis (Temporal Arteritis) if left untreated?
a: Irreversible vision loss (anterior ischemic optic neuropathy).

q: What is the immediate next step in management for a patient strongly suspected of having Giant Cell Arteritis with visual symptoms?
a: Start high-dose IV glucocorticoids immediately (do not wait for temporal artery biopsy results).

What triad of clinical manifestations characterizes Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (GPA / Wegener's)?
a: Upper respiratory tract involvement (e.g., sinusitis, saddle nose), lower respiratory tract involvement (e.g., cavitary lung nodules), and glomerulonephritis.

q: Which autoantibody is highly specific for Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (GPA)?
What features distinguish Eosinophilic Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (EGPA / Churg-Strauss) from other vasculitides?
a: Asthma, allergic rhinitis, peripheral blood eosinophilia, and p-ANCA (anti-Myeloperoxidase / anti-MPO) positivity.

What are the classic laboratory criteria for Antiphospholipid Syndrome (APS)?
a: Lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin antibodies, and anti-β<sub>2</sub>-glycoprotein I antibodies.

q: A patient with suspected Antiphospholipid Syndrome (APS) may have what paradoxical laboratory finding?
a: Prolonged PTT that does not correct with a mixing study (due to lupus anticoagulant), despite being a pro-thrombotic state.

q: What is the classic presentation of Adult-Onset Still's Disease?
a: Quotidian (daily spiking) fevers, evanescent salmon-colored maculopapular rash, inflammatory arthritis, and markedly elevated ferritin.

What is the treatment for severe Lupus Nephritis?
a: High-dose glucocorticoids combined with an immunosuppressant such as Mycophenolate Mofetil or Cyclophosphamide.
